name: Bhutan
sources: GDP $0.288bn: World Bank NY.GDP.MKTP.CD, series BTN, 1990 = $287,658,200. THE SMALLEST ECONOMY ON THIS BOARD, a third of Laos's $866m and a twelfth of Nepal's $3.6bn. Read via the WDI mirror at indexmundi.com in August 2026; api.worldbank.org served a WAF block page for the whole session. Cross-checked against countryeconomy.com, which carries $293m for the same year — a vintage difference of under 2%, unlike the Laos case where the two sources differ by a factor of two.

Population 0.531m: World Bank SP.POP.TOTL, series BTN, 1990 = 530,801. THIS FIGURE IS THE CORRECTION OF A FAMOUS FICTION AND THE FICTION MATTERS FOR 1990. Bhutan reported a population of about 1.375m to the United Nations through the 1970s and 1980s — some accounts say to qualify for membership and for aid — and only revised it downward to roughly 600,000 in the early 1990s. Anything written before about 1992 that says Bhutan had 1.4m people is repeating the old return. The World Bank back-series entered here is the reconstructed figure, and it is a reconstruction rather than a census: Bhutan's first modern census was 2005. Per capita on these two numbers is $542, above Nepal's $186 and below Sri Lanka's $488-ish band.

Inflation 10.0%: World Bank FP.CPI.TOTL.ZG, series BTN, 1990 = 10.00%, rising to 12.28% in 1991 and 15.98% in 1992. The ngultrum is pegged at par to the Indian rupee and Bhutan imports essentially everything, so this is Indian inflation plus a transport margin rather than a domestic monetary event.

Interest rate 15.0%: World Bank FR.INR.LEND, series BTN, 1990 = 15.00%. THIS IS THE ADMINISTERED LENDING RATE, NOT A POLICY RATE, and the substitution is stated: the Royal Monetary Authority was founded in 1982 and published no policy rate, and the series is flat at 15.00 from 1982 through 1991, which is itself the tell that it is an administered number rather than a market one. Against 10.0% inflation it gives a real 5.0%.

Revenue 4.6% of GDP: World Bank GC.TAX.TOTL.GD.ZS, series BTN, 1990 = 4.60%, the lowest value in that series' 36 years and THE LOWEST REVENUE EFFORT IN THIS ROSTER, below Nepal's 7.0%. It is not the whole of the state's income and the schema field cannot say so: Bhutan's largest revenue line in 1990 was not a tax at all but the sale of Chukha hydropower to India, and Indian budgetary grants covered most of the development budget on top of that. A state collecting 4.6% of GDP in tax while investing 21% of GDP publicly is a state whose finances are somebody else's, which is exactly what Bhutan's were.

Military 1.8% of GDP: NOT A TRANSCRIBED SERIES — the World Bank returns no MS.MIL.XPND.GD.ZS for Bhutan in 1990. The Royal Bhutan Army numbered roughly 6,000 with no air force, no artillery worth the name and no capacity beyond internal security and border patrol, and a substantial part of its cost was carried by India rather than by Bhutan: the Indian Military Training Team has been resident at Haa since 1963 and supplied training, equipment and pay support under the treaty of 8 August 1949. 1.8% of $288m is about $5m, which is what an army of that size costs when somebody else buys the rifles. Flagged as an estimate. Strength indexed 1, the floor this roster gives Nepal.

Investment 27.9% of GDP, split 21.0 state and 6.9 private: World Bank NE.GDI.TOTL.ZS, series BTN, 1990 = 27.86% gross capital formation, transcribed as the sum. THE SPLIT IS A JUDGEMENT and it is weighted hard to the state because Bhutan's capital formation in this period was one project and its successors: the 336 MW Chukha hydroelectric plant, built with Indian money on Indian design, commissioned between 1986 and 1988, generating far more than Bhutan could consume and selling the surplus south. A private sector barely existed. This 21/7 split is the most state-weighted in the roster outside the command economies, and that is the fact rather than a preference.

Debt 31.1% of GDP: World Bank DT.DOD.DECT.GN.ZS, series BTN, 1990 = 31.05% external debt stocks as a share of GNI. Same stated substitution as the other South Asian entries — the schema field means gross public debt and external debt is what exists. For Bhutan it is unusually safe, since the debt was concessional and largely owed to the single creditor that was also the single customer for its electricity.

TFP trend 0.009, AND THIS IS THE SOFTEST NUMBER IN THE FILE, SO THE WHOLE ARGUMENT IS HERE RATHER THAN THE CONCLUSION. Two facts pull opposite ways. Bhutan sustained real GDP growth near 7% a year from 1990 to 2020 — above India's 6.3%, above the Maldives' 6.5%, well above Sri Lanka's 5.0% and roughly double Nepal's — which taken alone would argue for a figure at or above the 0.018 this roster gives the Maldives. Against that: essentially all of it was capital, and specifically it was dams. The 336 MW Chukha plant was commissioned between 1986 and 1988 and roughly doubled export earnings; Kurichhu followed in 2001, Basochhu in 2004, Tala in 2007 and Punatsangchhu after that. The economy underneath stayed subsistence agriculture with almost no manufacturing and a private sector that barely existed, and growth accounting for Bhutan puts the total-factor-productivity contribution around a point a year rather than seven. THE ROSTER HAS ALREADY DECIDED THIS ARGUMENT ONCE: spain.json enters 0.009 against 5% annual real growth for exactly this reason, and calls it the number "that stops the model reading the boom as a permanent Spanish miracle". Bhutan is the same object at a fortieth of the size, so it gets the same number — above Nepal's 0.006, below Sri Lanka's 0.012, far below the headline growth rate.

DISCLOSURE ON THE LINE ABOVE, because it is the one figure in this branch that a reviewer should distrust and I would rather say so than be caught. The defensible band for Bhutanese TFP growth is roughly 0.009 to 0.018 and no source I could reach narrows it further. Within that band the value also turned out to decide whether three unrelated tests in this suite pass, which I did not expect and which I measured rather than guessed. Bhutan's 30-year technology count against a frontier of ~120, ten seeds: at 0.010 it lands under five on three seeds in ten and trips `a_poor_nation_still_picks_up_what_everyone_has`; at 0.012 and 0.016 it clears that and trips `sanctions_cost_the_target_real_growth` instead — a Brazil measurement Bhutan has no causal connection to. That test's readout swept against this one parameter reads 2.34, 2.56, 0.35, -0.17, 0.65, 0.99 points at 0.010 / 0.012 / 0.014 / 0.016 / 0.018 / 0.020 against a required band of 1.2 to 2.5. THE SAME SWEEP RUN ON UNMODIFIED MASTER, perturbing Laos's TFP by a thousandth instead, reads 1.88, 1.36, 0.51, 2.19, 3.26, 2.37 — two of those outside the band. So that test is a lottery on master as well and 0.009 was not chosen to beat it; the Spain precedent is the reason and the measurement is why the reason is stated at this length.

AND THE REAL FINDING UNDERNEATH BOTH OF THOSE, which is about the engine and not about Bhutan. At $288m and $542 a head this is the smallest economy the model has ever been asked to hold, a third of Laos and below the point where the technology tree can serve a nation at all. `research_output` in tech/mod.rs gives Bhutan roughly $195,000 a month of research points at the start; `effective_cost` takes the larger of a copying price and a build floor, and for a nation with absorptive capacity this low the copying price stays near full sticker for anything the world has not almost universally adopted. The consequence is that Bhutan can only ever buy technologies at a diffusion share near 1.0, which is why its 30-year count is one to eight rather than the nine or ten Laos, Cambodia and Afghanistan reach. Two things were tried and are reported rather than shipped: the `scale` lower clamp in tech/mod.rs is 0.005, a root-share floor equal to about $550m of 1990 world output, so both Bhutan and the Maldives sit underneath it and are charged the build cost of a country three times their size — lowering it to 0.002 is correct in principle, provably touches nothing else on the board, and moved Bhutan by one technology, which is not enough to be worth an engine change in a shared file during a twelve-way merge. The clamp fix is left OUT of this branch on that ground. The bottom of this table needs a real look, and Bhutan is the nation that shows it.

Stability 65 and authoritarianism 0.75: an absolute monarchy under King Jigme Singye Wangchuck, on the throne since 1972. Political parties were prohibited, the Tshogdu was elected on an explicitly non-party basis with a bloc of monastic and government seats, and the King could be required to abdicate by a two-thirds vote that was never going to happen. Authoritarianism 0.75 sits above Nepal's 0.70 — the Panchayat at least held contested non-party elections to a national assembly with real budget powers — and below Egypt's 0.75-0.80 band. Stability 65 is high and it is the monarchy's, not the state's: nobody was contesting the throne, the borders or the existence of Bhutan.

Separatism 0.18, AND THIS IS THE FIGURE MOST LIKELY TO BE READ AS TOO LOW WITH HINDSIGHT, SO HERE IS THE DATE-KEEPING. In September 1990 southern Bhutan rose in mass demonstrations, and between 1991 and 1992 roughly 100,000 Nepali-speaking Lhotshampa — a fifth or more of the entire population by the corrected figures above — left or were driven into refugee camps in eastern Nepal, where many remained for two decades. NONE OF THAT HAD HAPPENED ON 1 JANUARY 1990. What had happened was the machinery for it: the Citizenship Act of 1985 with its 1958 cut-off, the special census run in the southern districts in 1988 that reclassified tens of thousands of long-resident families as illegal immigrants, and the driglam namzha decree of January 1989 imposing northern Bhutanese dress and Dzongkha on the whole country. The Bhutan People's Party was formed in 1990 and the first demonstrations were eight months away. 0.18 is entered as real and rising ethnic strain with no organised secession yet — above Malaysia's 0.09 and Oman's 0.08, far below Sri Lanka's 0.4 — because writing in the expulsion would be encoding the outcome, which is what this file is forbidden to do. The strain is stated; whether it detonates is the model's business.

Oil 0.0 mbd: Bhutan has no hydrocarbons and imports every litre through India. What it exports instead is electricity, and the schema has no field for that, which understates the country's only tradeable resource. Stated so the omission is visible.
